paper_metadata.title: A Semantic Best-Effort Approach for Extracting Structured Discourse Graphs from Wikipedia
paper_metadata.abstract: Most information extraction approaches available today have either focused on the extraction of simple relations or in scenarios where data extracted from texts should be normalized into a database schema or ontology. Some relevant information present in natural language texts, however, can be irregular, highly contextualized, with complex semantic dependency relations, poorly structured, and intrinsically ambiguous. These characteristics should also be supported by an information extraction approach. To cope with this scenario, this work introduces a semantic best-effort information extraction approach, which targets an information extraction scenario where text information is extracted under a pay-as-you-go data quality perspective, trading high-accuracy, schema consistency and terminological normalization for domain-independency, context capture, wider extraction scope and maximization of the text semantics extraction and representation. A semantic information extraction framework (Graphia) is implemented and evaluated over the Wikipedia corpus.

problem_addressed: The paper addresses extraction of irregular, contextualized, semantically dependent, poorly structured, and ambiguous information from unstructured text into RDF-compatible structured discourse graphs. Its objective is to maximize text-semantic coverage and context capture under a pay-as-you-go quality perspective, accepting lower accuracy, schema consistency, and terminological normalization than conventional ontology- or database-oriented information extraction.

methodology.description: Graphia implements a sequential semantic-best-effort pipeline. It parses English Wikipedia sentences into Stanford PCFG syntactic C-Structures; resolves named entities with DBpedia Spotlight and a local TF/IDF DBpedia URI index; resolves personal, possessive, and reflexive coreferences using gender/number agreement and text-distance heuristics; maps annotated C-Structures to sentence-level triple trees using DFS syntactic transformation rules; detects explicit and implicit temporal references; and serializes the triple trees as an RDF-compatible graph with context URIs and local URIs for unresolved resources. The representation uses named and non-named entities, properties, quantifiers and generic operators, triple trees, reification, temporal context, coreference links, and resolved or normalized entities. The method prioritizes broad semantic representation and interpretability of graph fragments over completeness and strict normalization.

ontology_or_schema_use.value: The output is an RDF-based Structured Discourse Graph representation rather than a strictly normalized domain ontology. Named entities map to RDF instances, non-named entities map to classes that may also be referenced as instances through punning, and named entities may be linked to DBpedia URIs. The approach deliberately trades schema consistency and terminological normalization for context capture and wider coverage; unresolved resources receive local URIs.

evaluation.setting: Manual evaluation of graphs generated from five randomly selected English Wikipedia articles: two people, two organizations, and one place, each exceeding 40K characters. Ill-formed sentences and sentences outside the pipeline scope, including complex subordination structures, were removed. Human evaluators inspected the original sentence and graph visualization, classified ten sentence features, nine error categories, and graph correctness/completeness/interpretability.

value: Across 150 sentences and 1033 extracted relations, the average correctness was 44.8%, completeness was 16.2%, and interpretability was 95.6%.
The most frequent average error categories were triple-tree construction (0.280), object construction (0.244), and reification construction (0.132).
Named-entity errors averaged 0.056 and explicit-temporal-reference errors averaged 0.110; the paper characterizes these semantic pivots as comparatively robust.
The paper reports that 55.2% of graphs contained some extraction error, while 95.6% retained a correct basic triple path sufficient for interpretation.
The paper attributes low completeness mainly to partial extraction and ignored non-central structures such as appositives.

value: Author-reported strength: the SDG representation captures semantic context and dependencies while remaining RDF-compatible and navigable back to the source text.
Author-reported strength: isolation between extraction structures limits the semantic impact of incomplete or erroneous components and preserves interpretable graph fragments.
Experimental result: 95.6% of evaluated graphs were interpretable at the basic subject-predicate-object path level.
Review-level interpretation: the method covers entity linking, coreference, temporal context, reification, and complex discourse structure beyond simple binary open-relation extraction.

evidence.excerpt: This isolation facilitates the data consumption/interpretation process... where the impact of possible incomplete or erroneous extractions is minimized.
The extractor is able to extract an informational and correct fragment in practically all the sentences.
The proposed representation supported the best-effort extraction by isolating errors from different parts of the extraction pipeline.

value: Experimental weakness: only 44.8% of graphs were fully correct and only 16.2% were complete.
The extraction rules ignore or partially process some non-central sentence structures, including appositives, reducing completeness.
Object construction, especially for non-named entities, is a major error source.
Triple-tree and reification construction remain error-prone, particularly for prepositional phrases.

Review-level interpretation: the approach relies heavily on parser output, hand-designed syntactic rules, heuristic coreference, and external entity-linking services, limiting robustness for structures outside the supported scope.

evidence.excerpt: Only 16.2% of the extracted graphs mapped all the information contained in the sentence.
The major impacting error categories were triple trees, object and reification construction.
The evaluation of error categories shows that this can be achieved by improving non-named entity recognition criteria and the treatment of prepositional phrases.

value: The extractor has limited completeness because it often ignores sentence structures that are not central, such as appositives, and performs partial extraction.
The breadth of rules for extracting prepositional phrases is limited, causing relatively frequent reification-construction errors.
The paper excludes complex subordination structures from evaluation because they are outside the pipeline scope.
The representation's emphasis on context makes reification, named graphs, quads, and quints central and leaves open representational issues for text semantics.

value: Author-stated improvement: increase extraction completeness.
Author-stated improvement: improve non-named entity recognition criteria.
Author-stated improvement: improve treatment of prepositional phrases and reification construction.
Review-level proposed improvement: expand syntactic rule coverage and evaluate complex subordination rather than excluding it.
Review-level proposed improvement: replace or augment heuristic coreference and linking with broader, error-aware models while retaining provenance and component isolation.

evidence.excerpt: The final approach showed a high coverage of the elements of the SDG representation model, with the evaluation pointing into a main direction for improvement: increasing the extraction completeness.
This can be achieved by improving non-named entity recognition criteria and the treatment of prepositional phrases.

value: The paper leaves unresolved how to obtain high completeness while preserving the semantic-best-effort strategy and interpretability.
Complex and composite sentence structures, especially complex subordination, remain outside the demonstrated extraction scope.
Non-named entity recognition, object construction, and prepositional-phrase/reification extraction remain major unresolved technical problems.
The paper identifies unresolved representational questions around context-heavy RDF modeling, including reifications, named graphs, quads, and quints.
Review-level inference: the method does not establish how well the pipeline transfers beyond English Wikipedia or domains lacking DBpedia coverage.

code_and_data_availability: The paper names the Graphia extraction framework and gives a Graphia URL; it also refers to online details of the graph-extraction algorithm. The paper does not report a source-code repository, license, downloadable release, or dataset release. The evaluation corpus consists of selected Wikipedia articles, but no packaged dataset is reported.
